original_question: Let σ = (σij), 1 ⩽ i ̸= j ⩽ n, be an irreducible elementary net(carpet) of order n ⩾ 3 over a field K(see 19.48). The net σ is said to be closed if the elementary net subgroup E(σ) does not contain new elementary transvections. The net σ is said to be completable if its diagonal can be supplemented with subgroups to a complete net. Completable elementary nets are closed. It is known that over fields of characteristic 0 and 2 there exist irreducible closed elementary nets that are not completable(V. A. Koibaev, Trudy Inst. Mat. Mekh. Ural Div. Ross. Akad. Nauk, 17, no. 4(2011), 134–141(Russian); V. A. Koibaev, Siberian Math. J., 62, no. 2(2021), 262–266). Do there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order n ⩾ 3 over a field of odd characteristic that are not completable?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.76 in the 21st issue (2026) of The Kourovka Notebook, with notation and the basic definitions imported from Problem 19.48 in the 19th issue (2018).
correct_elements: Your draft already targets the correct problem almost verbatim: it matches Problem 21.76 rather than the earlier Problem 19.48 itself. It correctly keeps the scope narrow: irreducible elementary nets (carpets), order n >= 3, a field of odd characteristic, closedness defined via the elementary net subgroup E(σ), completability defined by adding diagonal subgroups, and the known contrast with characteristics 0 and 2.
missing_details: It is not fully stand-alone, because it relies on the cross-reference 'see 19.48' instead of restating the underlying definition of an elementary net (carpet) of order n over a field K.
It does not explicitly restate that irreducible means that all off-diagonal subgroups σij are nontrivial.

It uses E(σ) without defining the elementary net subgroup; to be stand-alone, one should identify it as the subgroup generated by the elementary transvections corresponding to the off-diagonal entries.

It says 'completable' but does not spell out what a complete net is; namely, one needs the existence of diagonal additive subgroups σii that make the full family (σij)1<=i,j<=n satisfy the net multiplication conditions for all indices.

The existential quantifiers are implicit; the official problem asks whether there exist some field K of odd characteristic and some n >= 3 for which such a closed but non-completable irreducible elementary net exists.

For maximum fidelity to the notebook, the wording 'new elementary transvections' can be normalized to the notebook's own terminology ('new' in 21.76; 'additional' in 19.48), though this does not change the mathematical content.
refined_question: Does there exist a field K of odd characteristic (equivalently, char K = p > 2), an integer n >= 3, and an irreducible elementary net (carpet) σ = (σij)1<=i!=j<=n over K such that each σij is a nonzero additive subgroup of K, the off-diagonal net relations σirσrj ⊆ σij hold whenever i, r, j are pairwise distinct, the elementary net subgroup E(σ) = < tij(α) = I + αeij : α in σij, i != j > contains no new elementary transvections tij(β) with β not in σij (so σ is closed), but there do not exist additive subgroups σii ⊆ K for 1 <= i <= n such that the full family (σij)1<=i,j<=n satisfies σirσrj ⊆ σij for all i, r, j (so σ is not completable)?
justification: The exact target is Problem 21.76, not Problem 19.48. Your draft reproduces the wording of 21.76 almost exactly, including the explicit cross-reference back to 19.48 for the notions of net/carpet, elementary net, irreducible, and closed. Problem 21.76 is the official sharpened version in the notebook: it introduces 'completable', records that counterexamples are known in characteristics 0 and 2, and asks specifically whether analogous irreducible closed but non-completable elementary nets exist over fields of odd characteristic. Problem 19.48 is only the earlier background problem defining the notation and asking a different question about closedness under an R-module hypothesis. Also, this arXiv item is a problem collection rather than a standard article with labels such as Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, and Theorem 1.3; here the nearest official formulation is the numbered open problem 21.76, with definitions from 19.48.
